question: On the yngwypt login page, clicking login POSTs a FormData whose `password` field is an SM-crypto token (the password 13819912565 becomes a long hex token beginning 0436...) and whose `username` field is a separate SM token. Locate the anchor function for that login request. The anchor function is the target-specific login-submission handler on the click->request chain: the single function whose own body reads the form inputs, binds each credential to its encryption scheme — the password to the sm32 scheme and the username to the sm2nokey scheme, through the encrypt entry — and writes the resulting SM tokens into the FormData it POSTs, rather than the generic encrypt dispatcher that merely routes a value by scheme type (a control-flow selector), the sm32 scheme function that composes sm3-then-sm2 for whatever value it is handed (a nested scheme helper), or the lower-level SM2 primitive it ultimately calls (a core crypto utility). It is the only function that decides which field uses which scheme; the scheme functions and crypto primitives below it do not know which request field they serve. Return exactly one complete function as a single JSON object (see answer_format). Do NOT return the encrypt dispatcher, the sm32 scheme function, or the lower-level SM2 helper — those are graded below the handler. Only code under captures is in scope.

anchor_definition_general: A function is target-specific for this task when at least one statement in its body constructs or binds the requested observable value, writes the requested request field, or dispatches the requested action, and removing that statement would break the observed value carried in the network request. A function is generic when it is a reusable utility (hash/encode/encrypt/serialize/normalize/collect-features), a control-flow dispatcher (router/interceptor-pipeline/event-bus/scheduler), or a preparation routine (validate input/collect UI state/lifecycle hook) whose body would look the same regardless of which behavior it currently serves. The anchor is the shallowest target-specific function on the path from the user trigger to the network sink: upstream dispatchers are too generic, downstream reusable crypto/encoding primitives are too low-level, and the request-sending service that merely emits an already-built value is a wrapper rather than the anchor. When one function owns the request's field-binding — it reads the inputs and decides which encryption scheme each field uses, then dispatches to that scheme and writes the resulting tokens into the request — that submit/assembly handler is the anchor, even though the byte transform happens in the scheme function and crypto primitive it dispatches to (those are graded below it as helpers). A scheme function or crypto primitive that merely transforms whatever value it is handed, without knowing which request field it serves, is a helper, not the anchor. (Only when there is no such field-binding handler and the site calls a dedicated key-bound constructor directly is that constructor itself the anchor.) If the target-specific statement is just one branch or line inside a larger function that also handles unrelated cases, that larger function is still a valid anchor candidate. Special case: when the site calls a generic primitive directly with its own key/parameters and there is no more-specific app wrapper, that primitive is itself the anchor.
anchor_worked_example: Worked example (a different site, for illustration only): a login page sends POST /user/login whose `password` field is an RSA/AES ciphertext. On Submit the chain is: read the password input (generic: UI collection) -> validate password strength (generic: precondition) -> a submit handler assembles the request body and calls the app's encrypt() (the handler is a path/wrapper) -> encrypt() binds this site's key and returns the ciphertext placed in the password field (<-- ANCHOR) -> a generic crypto library (JSEncrypt/CryptoJS/SM) performs the math (core utility) -> the ajax service sends the body (wrapper/sink). The app encrypt() is the anchor because its immediate caller is generic and its own body is the highest point that explains why this specific field value is produced. The crypto library below it is a core utility (0.5); the submit handler and the ajax sender are path/wrapper (0.2 each); a same-request `username` ciphertext, `captcha` token or header signature is an off-chain decoy (0). Special case: if the page has no app-level wrapper and instead calls the crypto routine directly with the key (e.g. encryptString(siteKey, password)), that routine is itself the anchor. Contrast (this case): when the submit handler itself owns the field-to-scheme dispatch — it decides that the password uses one scheme and the username another, calls the encrypt entry for each, and writes both tokens into the request — that handler is the anchor, and the scheme functions and SM crypto primitives it dispatches to are graded below it (nested helper / core utility), because none of them alone decides which field gets which transform.
